headline: Yields Too High to Ignore Lure Investors Back to Long-Dated Debt
author: George Nixon and Georgia Hall

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Long-dated government bonds spent much of the year punishing anyone brave enough to own them. Now yields are high enough that investors are coming back.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Risk-free payouts near multi-decade highs are becoming difficult to resist, particularly with stocks looking expensive and volatile. Ten-year US Treasuries yields peaked at almost 5.4% this month, their highest since 2002, while those in Japan reached a 30-year high of 3.14%.

The comeback trade in long bonds has enticed portfolio managers at JPMorgan Asset Management, Aegon Asset Management, Ninety One and Allianz GI, to name just a few. Yields are now in reverse, rewarding investors with a return of 2.2% in October on a gauge of global government bonds maturing in 10 years or more, a level that's handily beaten the flat performance of sovereign debt due in one to three years — and the first month since February in which longer bonds outperformed.

Those profits have encouraged investors to overlook, for now at least, the dangers that sent yields so high in the first place. Energy-driven inflation, tighter monetary policy and deteriorating government finances haven't disappeared. The price of taking those risks has simply become more attractive.
"The long-end just got too cheap and too unanchored," said JPMorgan Asset's head of global fixed income Bob Michele. He's been buying longer-dated from Australia and Japan as well as US Treasuries.

As investors question whether tech companies have overpromised on AI, government bonds are looking like a haven again. That's borne out by movement in and out of exchange traded funds. The iShares US Treasury Bond ETF drew inflows for the second consecutive month while the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF flipped to outflows from inflows the previous month.

To be sure, policy angst — Fed, Treasury and election-related — continues to weigh on demand for longer-dated US Treasuries. They sold off in reaction to the Fed's decision to leave interest rates unchanged, which rekindled doubt that Chairman Kevin Warsh is committed to the central bank's 2% inflation target.

Longer-dated European government debt also fell Thursday after investors interpreted comments from European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde to signal the central bank wouldn't intervene to stem a selloff caused by France's political and fiscal turmoil.

"I'd call it a pause rather than a turning point, as the pressures behind this year's selloff haven't gone away," said Hilary Winn, investment director at AJ Bell. "We still lean towards quality and shorter duration, rather than chase a long-dated rally."

Next month's US midterms give even bond bulls reason for caution. A divided Congress could put a lid on fiscal expansion and help long-dated Treasuries, while a surprise Republican hold of both chambers risks reopening the spending-and-inflation debate.

At the same time, an economic slowdown and flight to safety could pull yields lower, while looser fiscal policy or an escalation of the war that fuels inflation could trigger another selloff, said Oliver Faizallah, head of fixed-income research at Raymond James Wealth Management.
The long end of the Treasury market is "hard to get a good fair value on," Faizallah said.

Still, October's retreat in yields offers some relief to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ahead of his department's quarterly refunding statement, where it lays out its borrowing plans. Speculation has grown the US may cut sales of 20- and 30-year bonds, after yields on the latter soared to the highest since 2002. The rally reduces the urgency of that discussion, though many banks still expect such changes could come in 2027.

The appeal extends beyond the US. Higher yields are drawing buyers to long-dated Japanese bonds, while German debt is benefiting from a flight to safety amid France's turmoil. In the UK, reduced long-bond sales by the Bank of England and improving sentiment toward Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new government have helped long gilts outperform.

Royal London Asset Management moved to an overweight position on 30-year UK gilts over the past few months. Craig Inches, head of rates and cash, has been telling its clients it's the right time to extend duration.
"We've seen bond yields go higher, higher, higher, higher," Inches said.
